# Whole-continuous-space covers: attainment, normal stress, and zero total force

This note changes the feasible cover class. Above every relevant integer
index, the caps must cover all of `R^d`, not just its source fiber. This
removes supporting-fiber forces from the cap-circuit equations, but its
contact points need not belong to the source set. Neither that membership
nor an OC mass bound is asserted.

## 1. Fixed source and two cover classes

Let `n>=0,d>=1`, let `P subset Z^n` be finite and nonempty, and let
`K_z subset R^d` be full-dimensional compact convex bodies. Put

`S=union_z ({z} x K_z)`, `mu=sum_z vol_d|K_z`, `M=mu(S)>0`.

A cap has margin `L_i(z,x)=a_i dot z+u_i dot x-b_i`, with `|u_i|=1`.
Its hinge and mass are `Psi_i=int(L_i)_+ dmu` and `c_i=mu{L_i>=0}`.
All caps are closed and nonvertical; every `a_i` is an arbitrary real
integer-coordinate normal.

In the unframed class there are a fixed number of such caps, all with
variable unit continuous normal. In the framed class there are `N`
variable-normal caps and a further `2d` caps with fixed continuous
normals `+e_l,-e_l`, one of each for `l=1,...,d`. The frame caps have
FREE offsets and FREE integer tilts, just like the other caps. Their
masses and hinges are included in the constraints and objective.
No lower bound on a frame offset and no zero-mass constraint is imposed.

In either class the cover requirement is

`for every z in P, union_i {x:L_i(z,x)>=0}=R^d`.              (1)

The objective is `Psi=sum_i Psi_i`, and every cap must satisfy
`c_i<=tau M`. Adding the fixed frame to any existing whole-space cover
preserves (1). Initially each added cap can be made empty on `S` by
setting its integer tilt to zero and choosing a sufficiently large
finite offset. This adds no initial mass or hinge. At an optimum,
however, the frame caps are allowed to become nonempty; their zero
initial mass is not a lasting constraint.

## 2. Exact balanced certificate and attainment without a frame

For one base index, put `t_iz=b_i-a_i dot z`. Requirement (1) is
equivalent to the existence of `lambda_z in Delta` such that

`sum_i lambda_zi u_i=0`,
`sum_i lambda_zi t_iz<=0`.                                  (2)

One proof is the finite-dimensional alternative for strict affine
inequalities: the system `u_i dot x<t_iz` for every `i` has no solution
if and only if a nonzero nonnegative combination of the left-hand
normals vanishes and the same combination of the thresholds is
nonpositive. Normalize its coefficients to sum to one. Equivalently,
apply linear-program duality to

`F_z^infinity=inf_(x in R^d) max_i L_i(z,x)`:
`F_z^infinity=max_(lambda in Delta, sum lambda_i u_i=0)
                       [-sum_i lambda_i t_iz]`.             (3)

When (1) holds, the primal value is finite and nonnegative; both the
primal and dual linear programs attain their finite optima. In the
unframed class outside the feasible set, the primal can instead be
unbounded below. The certificate (2), which does not require evaluating
that infeasible case, is enough for the following compactness theorem.

**Attainment.** In either class, at a feasible fixed cap budget and cap
count, `Psi` attains a finite positive minimum.

Proof. Take a minimizing sequence with bounded hinges. Its thresholds
on each fiber are bounded below, and after a subsequence each tends to
a finite limit or to positive infinity. Unit variable normals converge;
frame normals remain fixed. This is the same estimate and finite-trace
compactification used in
the original hinge attainment proof (candidate de8d1a3251731edd).

Choose a certificate (2) for each fiber along the sequence, and take
limits of its simplex weights. A weight belonging to an infinite
threshold must tend to zero. Indeed, all other thresholds have one
common finite lower bound, whereas their weighted sum is nonpositive.
A weight bounded below at a threshold tending to infinity would
contradict that inequality. The limiting weights therefore sum to one
on finite-threshold coordinates and have zero continuous resultant.
Moreover their finite weighted threshold sum is nonpositive: for large
sequence indices the infinite-threshold terms are nonnegative, so
discarding them only decreases the original sum. Pass to the limit
in the finitely many remaining terms.

Saturate the infinite thresholds by large finite affine traces, leaving
all finite limits exact. The limiting certificate uses only the finite
coordinates, so it still proves (1). This saturation works separately
for each cap and preserves its fixed frame normal if there is one.
The hinges and cap masses converge exactly on the source fibers.
Thus the attained family obeys all budgets and covers whole `R^d`
above every `z`. Positivity follows from the inball lower bound for
actual-fiber covers, since (1) is the stronger condition. QED.

This attainment argument does not assert convergence or boundedness
of the minimizing contact points in `R^d`.

## 3. What the fixed frame supplies locally

In the framed class, `F_z^infinity` is finite and attained at EVERY
finite parameter value, and is locally Lipschitz in all free parameters.
To see this, let `T_z` bound the absolute values of the frame thresholds.
The maximum of the frame margins is at least

`|x|_infinity-T_z`.

The maximum of all margins at `x=0` is finite. Thus every minimizer
lies in a finite cube, with a bound uniform on a sufficiently small
parameter neighborhood. Choose a slightly larger cube. The full
linear program and the one restricted to this cube agree throughout
the neighborhood, and all optimal contacts lie strictly inside the
cube. Minimax on a fixed compact set now proves local Lipschitz
continuity, as in the original coverage lemma.

The fixed frame is essential to this particular unrestricted local
argument. Merely knowing that a limiting unframed cover satisfies (2)
does not prevent nearby variable normals from losing positive spanning,
in which case `F_z^infinity` can become negative infinity.

The common offset repair is exact:

`G=max(0,max_z(-F_z^infinity))`, `b_i^R=b_i-G`,
`F_z^infinity(Rp)=F_z^infinity(p)+G>=0`,
`|Rp-p|=sqrt(N+2d)G`.                                       (4)

All frame offsets must be free for (4). Restricting them to remain
outside the source would introduce additional boundary multipliers.

## 4. Generic-budget normality and exact sensitivity

Assume now that the source fibers are polytopes. Let `w(tau)` be the
attained framed whole-space-cover hinge value. Its feasible budget
domain is an upward interval. It is semialgebraic: source cap volumes
and hinges have finite rational polytope formulas, and coverage is
the finite quantified certificate (2), or the finite linear program
(3). Attainment lets the value graph be expressed by first-order real
quantifiers. Thus `w` is `C^1` and locally Lipschitz outside finitely
many interior feasible budgets.

At each such regular budget, every attained minimizer has normal
stress with objective multiplier one. The proof is exactly the two
penalty argument of
the generic-budget normality note (candidate 2d0fea5cdbf7c841),
using (4) and the local coercivity just proved. In its stronger form,
`Psi-w(max_i c_i/M)` has a local minimum among unbudgeted whole-space
covers if the budget is active. Repairing coverage yields normal
stationarity and

`M sum_i r_i=-w'(tau)`.                                     (5)

At a slack minimizing budget, `w'(tau)=0` and the direct coverage
repair gives `r_i=0`. All sums here and below include the frame caps.

The cap section gradients have the same consistent coarea form as
before, with densities between zero and one on supporting sections.
The coverage generalized gradients are convex combinations of actual
primal-dual saddle features

`lambda_i(z,x,-1)`.

This follows by the finite LP-basis argument on the local cube from
Section 3. Its artificial boundary has no active optimal contact.
Consequently each such saddle pair satisfies

`sum_i lambda_i u_i=0`.                                    (6)

At a multiplied active coverage constraint `F_z^infinity=0`, it also
satisfies

`L_i(z,x)<=0`, `lambda_i L_i(z,x)=0` for all `i`.             (7)

The point `(z,x)` may be outside `S`. It is an actual contact of the
whole-space cap arrangement, not necessarily a point of `K_z`.

## 5. Normal equations and the source-only force balance

Use the moment notation of the generic-budget note. A finite
probability measure `nu_z` on the saddle pairs supplies
`p_zi=int lambda_i dnu_z`, `q_zi=int lambda_i x dnu_z`.
There are nonnegative multipliers `eta_z,r_i` with active-constraint
complementarity, and for EVERY cap, including the fixed frame,

`W_i:=c_i+r_i S_i=sum_z eta_z p_zi`,                         (8)
`Z_i+r_i Z_i^s=sum_z eta_z z p_zi`.                          (9)

For each variable-normal cap only, its unit-normal stationarity and
the per-cap Euler cancellation give

`X_i+r_i X_i^s-sum_z eta_z q_zi=Psi_i u_i`.                 (10)

There is no assertion of (10) for a frame cap whose normal is fixed.
Its offset and integer-tilt equations (8)--(9), however, are fully
available. Combining them with (6) gives the exact identities

`sum_i W_i u_i=0`,                                         (11)
`sum_i u_i (Z_i+r_i Z_i^s)^T=0`,                           (12)
`sum_i W_i=sum_z eta_z`.                                   (13)

In contrast to the actual-fiber-cover system, (11) has no boundary
support-force term. Its reason is precisely the whole-space continuous
normal balance (6). Imposing one-sided constraints on the frame offsets
would spoil the derivation from (8), so they have deliberately been
left free.

There is a further scalar identity valid even for the fixed frame:

`w(tau)=sum_i u_i dot (X_i+r_i X_i^s)`.                     (14)

Indeed, (8)--(9) imply

`sum_i [a_i dot (Z_i+r_i Z_i^s)-b_i W_i]
 =sum_z eta_z int sum_i lambda_i(a_i dot z-b_i) dnu_z=0`.

The last equality follows from (6)--(7). On the source cap,
`a_i dot Z_i-b_i c_i=Psi_i-u_i dot X_i`; on its section,
`a_i dot Z_i^s-b_i S_i=-u_i dot X_i^s`. This proves (14).
It is also the stationarity identity for a common continuous dilation
of all halfspaces, which changes offsets and integer tilts but keeps
every unit continuous normal, including the frame, fixed.

Equations (11)--(14) involve only actual source cap and section
moments on their left sides. They do not give a cap mass estimate by
themselves. Contact barycenters outside `K_z` prevent importing the
same-real-base bounded-displacement argument from the actual-fiber
cover system.

## 6. Right continuity and exceptional budgets

The same threshold and balanced-certificate compactness proves that
`w` is right-continuous at every feasible budget. It is nonincreasing
and semialgebraic. Hence for interior feasible `a<b`,

`w(a)-w(b)
 = M integral_a^b sum_i r_i(t) dt
   +sum_(a<t<=b)[w(t-)-w(t)]`.                             (15)

The proof is the one in the sensitivity note: integrate on the finitely
many regular intervals and keep every downward jump. No selection of
the individual multiplier measures is needed to define the scalar
integrand, which equals `-w'(t)/M`.

## 7. Bounded hinges do not bound whole-space contacts

Here is an exact limitation even with a fixed frame and a strictly
feasible cap budget. Let `n=0,d=2`, let the source be the square
`K=[-1,1]^2`, of mass four. For `0<epsilon<=1/8` define

`s=sqrt(1+epsilon^2)`, `delta=1/4`, `B=s delta/epsilon`.

Take two variable-normal margins

`L_1(x,y)=x`,
`L_2(x,y)=(-x+epsilon y)/s+delta`,

and the four fixed-frame margins `x-B,-x-B,y-B,-y-B`.
The frame is empty on the source since `B>1`. The whole-space minimum
is zero, at the UNIQUE contact

`(x,y)=(0,-B)`.                                            (16)

To verify this directly, a point with all margins nonpositive must
satisfy `x<=0`, `x>=epsilon y+s delta`, and `y>=-B`.
The last two imply `x>=0`, so `x=0` and `y=-B`. Conversely (16)
has its first, second, and `-y-B` margins zero and its other frame
margins negative. Those three normals admit positive balanced weights:
take unnormalized weights `1/s,1,epsilon/s`. Their weighted margin
is identically zero, since `delta-(epsilon/s)B=0`. Thus the maximum
margin is nonnegative everywhere and vanishes exactly at (16).

The first cap has mass two and hinge one. For the second cap the
line `x=epsilon y+s delta` lies strictly between `-1` and `1` for
every `y in [-1,1]`, so direct integration gives

`c_2=2(1+s delta)`,
`Psi_2=[(1+s delta)^2+epsilon^2/3]/s`.                       (17)

Its normalized mass is `(1+s/4)/2<2/3`, because `s<4/3`.
Thus all six caps satisfy the strict fixed budget `tau=2/3`.
Their total hinge tends to `1+25/16=41/16`, while the unique
whole-space contact (16) escapes to infinity as `epsilon downarrow0`.
The limiting source traces of the two principal caps already cover
the plane, but their limiting contact geometry is different.

This example concerns feasible covers, not minimizing covers. It
proves that hinge boundedness alone does not control whole-space
contacts, and that the stronger local-gradient compactification from
the actual-fiber setting cannot be transferred merely by inspecting
traces on `S`. Whole-space attainment in Section 2 remains valid
because its proof uses balanced dual weights instead of contacts.

## 8. Exact scope

The framed class has at most the original cap count plus `2d` caps.
The added directions secure coercivity and a generic-budget normal
system. Their offsets remain free and their budgets remain genuine
parts of the optimization. It has not been proved that the added
caps retain zero source mass at a minimizer, or that they can be
removed from a final quantitative bound.

Whole-space attainment needs no frame, but the unrestricted local
normality proof above does. Its new invariant is the exact zero total
continuous normal force (11), together with its base-moment version
(12), scalar dilation identity (14), and sensitivity formula (5).
The price is that the contact points are not required to belong to
the source fibers. No claim resolving that tradeoff is made here.
